title: Da Vinci Code
def: A 2003 novel and 2006 film claiming that the divinity of Jesus was invented at Nicaea; historians reject its claims.
what: Dan Brown’s The Da Vinci Code says that the Council of Nicaea in 325 voted Jesus into divinity. Some Muslim writers have welcomed it as supporting the view that Christian doctrine departed from Jesus’ teaching. Historians point out that Christians had worshipped Jesus as divine long before Nicaea and that the council’s argument was over a precise definition of his relation to the Father.
sources: Muslims need not rely on a novel. Their own argument from the Quran and the Gospels is made on its own terms, and does not depend on a theory about Constantine.

title: Dajjal
def: The False Messiah of the end of time, described in hadith but not named in the Quran.
what: Dajjāl means “the great deceiver”. Hadith describe a one-eyed man who will appear before the end of time and claim to be a lord, and who will work wonders and spread corruption. Jesus will descend and kill him, as in a report in Sahih Muslim. The Prophet taught believers to seek God’s protection from him in every prayer, and said that reciting the opening verses of chapter 18 guards against him (Sahih Muslim).
misread: That Muslims have copied the Christian idea of the Antichrist.
sources: The word “Dajjal” is applied also to impostors in general: the Prophet said that thirty liars would arise, each claiming to be a prophet (Sahih al-Bukhari). The ideas of an end-time deceiver and of Jesus’ return are found in Judaism, Christianity and Islam, and Muslims see this as a sign that they come from a common source.

title: Dar al-Islam and Dar al-Harb
def: Classical legal terms dividing the world into the “house of Islam” and the “house of war”, which are not in the Quran or hadith.
what: Jurists of the eighth and ninth centuries, among them the Hanafi al-Shaybani, used “house of Islam” for lands under Muslim law and “house of war” for those at war with them. A third category, the “house of treaty” (dār al-ṣulḥ), was added for lands at peace with Muslim rulers. The terms arose from the political division of the age.
misread: That Islam holds the non-Muslim world to be in a permanent state of war.
sources: The terms are legal constructs and not revelation, and many scholars today regard them as outdated. Muslims live as citizens in many countries and are told to keep their covenants (5:1). Contemporary scholars have offered other terms, such as “house of covenant” or “house of testimony”.

title: Dates
def: The date palm is named often in the Quran and was the food Mary was told to eat in labour (19:25).
what: Date palms are among God’s signs for growth (36:34, 50:10, 55:11). Mary, in labour, is told “shake the trunk of the palm toward you, it will drop fresh ripe dates upon you” (19:25). The Prophet used to break his fast with fresh dates, or dry ones if there were none (Abu Dawud).

title: David
def: King David, honoured in the Quran as a prophet and king to whom God gave the Psalms.
what: The Quran says God gave David the Zabur (4:163, 17:55), made him a ruler on earth (38:26), taught him to make coats of mail (21:80) and made mountains and birds echo his praises (21:79, 38:18–19). He killed Goliath (2:251). The Prophet said that David’s was the best fast, on alternate days, and the best prayer, at one half of the night (Sahih al-Bukhari).
sources: The Quran presents David as one who sinned and repented, “and he fell down bowing and turned in repentance” (38:24). It does not tell the story of Bathsheba and Uriah as the Bible does, and Muslim scholars reject the claim that a prophet committed adultery or murder.

title: Dawah
def: “Invitation”: calling people to Islam, which the Quran says should be done by wisdom and good counsel.
what: “Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good counsel, and argue with them in the way that is best” (16:125). The Prophet’s task, in the Quran, was to convey, not to compel: “your duty is only to convey” (13:40, 5:99). Muslims perform it by speech, writing, charity and example.

title: Dead Sea Scrolls
def: Hebrew manuscripts found near the Dead Sea from 1947, dated from about 250 BC to AD 70.
what: The scrolls include almost every book of the Hebrew Bible. The great Isaiah scroll is about a thousand years older than the earlier manuscripts known before it, and differs from them in small ways. They also include sectarian writings.
sources: Muslim writers have used them in two directions: as showing that the Hebrew text was transmitted with care, which some say answers the charge of wholesale alteration, and as showing variants. The Quran’s own claim concerns the Torah that Moses was given and the Jews’ “distortion of words” (4:46), which scholars read in several ways (see Tahrif).

title: Death
def: The Quran says every soul will taste death (3:185), and that God created death as well as life as a test.
what: “Every soul will taste death” (3:185). “He who created death and life to test you, which of you is best in deed” (67:2). The Quran says that when the angel of death comes the soul is taken, and the righteous are met with peace (16:32). Burial in the earth is described as God’s mercy (80:21).
misread: That death is the result of Adam’s sin.
sources: In the Quran death is not a curse from Adam’s fall. Before the fall God had already said He would place on earth a successor (2:30). Adam’s mistake was forgiven (2:37), and the Quran says all are to be brought back to God.

title: Debates
def: Muslims and Christians have debated their beliefs since the early centuries, sometimes in the courts of the caliphs.
what: A famous example is the discussion between the Nestorian patriarch Timothy I and the caliph al-Mahdi in Baghdad in about 781, which was conducted with courtesy on both sides. John of Damascus and Theodore Abu Qurra wrote in the same period. In modern times the South African teacher Ahmad Deedat took part in many public debates, including that with the American preacher Jimmy Swaggart in 1986.

title: Deception
def: “God is the best of schemers” (3:54): makr means a plan or counter-plan, and the verse is about God defeating the plots of those who plotted against Jesus.
what: In the Quran makara and makr are used of plotting by people, and of God’s response (3:54, 8:30). In 3:54 the context is the plot against Jesus: “they plotted, and God plotted, and God is the best of plotters.” The word in Arabic can mean “plan” in a neutral sense, and in this context means a counter-plan.
misread: That the Quran describes God as a deceiver.
sources: Commentators such as al-Tabari and al-Razi explain it as a rhetorical echo: God’s defeat of the plot is called by the same word as the plot itself, as with the Arabic idiom of answering in kind. The Quran describes God as truthful (4:122) and lists the qualities of truthfulness among His names. A thing done by God is never deceit.

title: Deedat, Ahmad
def: A South African teacher of Indian origin (1918–2005) known for debates and writings on Muslim-Christian questions.
what: Ahmad Deedat founded the Islamic Propagation Centre International in Durban and wrote short books such as Christ in Islam and Crucifixion or Cruci-fiction?. He received the King Faisal International Prize in 1986. Some Muslims admire his work and others criticise its confrontational tone.

title: Deeds
def: The Quran says deeds are weighed (21:47) and that faith without good works is incomplete; the Prophet said the best are those done regularly even if small.
what: “We will set up the scales of justice on the Day of Resurrection, and no soul will be wronged in the least” (21:47). The Prophet said “the most beloved deeds to God are the most regular, even if few” (Sahih al-Bukhari). He told Aisha of a woman who prayed all night, and said: “do what you can bear; God does not tire until you tire” (Sahih al-Bukhari).

title: Deification
def: The Quran’s charge that some of the People of the Book made a god of Jesus (5:72–73), and the Christian reply that this is not what the Church teaches.
what: The Quran says that “those who say that God is the Messiah, son of Mary, have disbelieved” (5:72), and has Jesus say: “Worship God, my Lord and your Lord” (5:72). Christians answer that they do not say Jesus is a creature made into God, but that God became man. Muslims reply that, whatever the doctrine’s wording, they cannot accept that the Creator took on human nature.
sources: The Quran calls Jesus “a messenger” and “His servant” (4:171–172) and has him deny, on the Day of Judgement, that he told people to take him and his mother as gods (5:116). The two sides agree on God’s mercy and on Jesus’ place in it, and differ on what Jesus is.

title: Desecration of the Quran
def: Muslims hold the Quran in great respect, and burning or defiling a copy gives deep offence; scholars have criticised violent reactions.
what: Muslims handle the Quran with care, do not put it on the floor, and traditionally wash before touching it. Reports that a copy was desecrated, such as those from Guantanamo Bay in 2005 or the burning of copies by individuals in the West, have caused riots in which people were killed.
sources: Muslim scholars and leaders have often condemned the violence. The Prophet bore the insults of those who mocked the revelation, and the Quran instructs: “if you hear God’s verses being disbelieved and mocked, do not sit with them until they enter another topic” (4:140). A copy of the Quran cannot be harmed by an act of this kind, as Muslims believe God has promised to protect it (15:9).

title: Dhikr
def: Remembrance of God: reciting His names and praises, in prayer and at other times.
what: “O you who believe, remember God with much remembrance” (33:41). “Truly, in the remembrance of God do hearts find rest” (13:28). Common forms are subḥān Allāh (glory to God), al-ḥamdu li-llāh (praise be to God) and Allāhu akbar, which the Prophet recommended after each prayer thirty-three times each (Sahih al-Bukhari). Sufi orders use group recitation as a discipline.

title: Dhilla
def: Lowliness; the Quran uses it for the humiliation of wrongdoers and for the gentle humility believers should show each other and their parents.
what: The Quran says of the Israelites who turned away “humiliation and poverty were struck upon them” (2:61). It also describes the believers as “humble (adhilla) toward the believers, mighty against the disbelievers” (5:54), and tells children to “lower to your parents the wing of humility out of mercy” (17:24). Whether the word is blame or praise depends on the one it is applied to.

title: Dhimmi
def: A non-Muslim living under Muslim rule with the state’s pledge of protection.
what: Dhimma means a pledge or covenant. A dhimmi’s life, property and place of worship were protected by it, and the community ran its own courts and affairs by its own law. The Prophet is reported to have said that whoever kills a person under a treaty will not smell the fragrance of Paradise (Sahih al-Bukhari).
The Maliki jurist al-Qarafi (d. 1285) wrote that the pledge puts duties on Muslims: to treat them as neighbours under God’s protection, to defend them and to prevent their being wronged.
misread: That dhimmis were slaves, or hunted second-class people.
sources: The classical law did place distinctions and restrictions, and Muslims do not need to deny this. But the status was a legal one, with rights, and it compares well with how religious minorities were treated elsewhere in the same centuries. When the Jews were expelled from Spain in 1492, the Ottoman sultan Bayezid II received many of them. Nobody on this site claims the record was perfect, only that it was not what the caricature suggests.

The word “dhimmitude” is not a classical term. It was coined in the 1980s by the writer Bat Ye’or for what she describes as the condition of non-Muslims under Muslim rule, and historians dispute her generalisation. The record varies by period, place and ruler.

title: Dhu al-Kifl
def: A prophet named in the Quran among the steadfast (21:85, 38:48), whose identity is not given.
what: He is mentioned after Ishmael and Idris as among “the patient” (21:85–86) and “the best” (38:48). Commentators have identified him with Ezekiel, Elijah, Joshua or others, and some say he was a righteous man and not a prophet.

title: Din
def: “Religion”: the way of life and the accounting before God; also law, custom and obedience.
what: Dīn in the Quran means the religion God revealed (3:19, “the religion with God is Islam”), the Day of Judgement (yawm al-dīn, 1:4) and a way of life. Muhammad’s message is “the guidance and the religion of truth” (9:33). Muslims distinguish islām, submission to God; īmān, faith; and iḥsān, excellence.
sources: The verse “the religion with God is Islam” (3:19) uses the word in its general sense of submission to God, which the Quran says all the prophets practised: Abraham was “a Muslim” in this sense (3:67), and the apostles of Jesus said “we are Muslims” (3:52).

title: Dirham
def: A silver coin; the Quran says Joseph’s brothers sold him “for a miserable price, a few dirhams” (12:20).
what: The word dirham is from the Greek drachmē, which came into Arabic well before Islam, as the Arabs traded with Byzantium and Persia. The Quran says the price was “a few counted dirhams”, which can be read as a few silver pieces by weight.
misread: That the Quran puts a coin of a later age in the time of Joseph.
sources: The Quran is told in Arabic, for Arabic hearers, and its words for money are those of the hearers. Ancient trade used silver by weight long before coinage, and the Bible says that Joseph was sold for twenty shekels of silver (Genesis 37:28), a weight of silver. Translators do the same when they say “pieces of silver” of a time before coins.

title: Disability
def: The Quran lifts the burden of duties that a person cannot bear, and urges care for the blind, the sick and the weak.
what: “No blame is on the blind, nor on the lame, nor on the sick” (24:61; 48:17). When 4:95 said that those who sit at home were not equal to those who fight, the blind Companion Ibn Umm Maktum objected, and the words “except those who are disabled” were added (Sahih al-Bukhari). The Quran also tells guardians not to hand property to those who cannot manage it (4:5), and to treat them kindly.

title: Divination and the unseen
def: Knowledge of the unseen belongs to God alone (72:26), and divination is forbidden.
what: “He is the Knower of the unseen, and does not disclose His unseen to anyone” (72:26). The Quran counts the divining arrows among the abominations (5:90). The Prophet said: “Whoever goes to a fortune-teller and asks him about anything, his prayer will not be accepted for forty nights” (Sahih Muslim). The call to look to the stars for signs of the future was likewise condemned.

title: Divine attributes
def: How Muslims understand verses that speak of God’s hand, face or throne, without making Him like His creatures.
what: The Quran says “there is nothing like Him, and He is the Hearing, the Seeing” (42:11). It also speaks of His face (55:27), His hands (38:75), and of His rising over the Throne (20:5). Muslim scholars have understood these in different ways. The earliest scholars affirmed the words as they came and left the manner unknown: Malik ibn Anas is reported to have said, “the rising is known; how is unknown; belief in it is obligatory; asking about it is an innovation.” The Ash’aris and others interpret them in a figurative sense.
misread: That the Quran’s language makes Islam’s God a man-like being, in contradiction of its own statement.
sources: The two ideas are held together: affirming what scripture says, and denying likeness to creation. The Quran itself uses the human language of a hand or face as the Bible does, in order to speak of God to human beings.

title: Divorce
def: The Quran allows divorce, with a waiting period, reconciliation, witnesses, and provision for the wife.
what: A divorced woman waits three cycles before remarrying (2:228). A husband may take her back within that time (2:229–231), and the Quran says: “retain them honourably or release them honourably” and tells the husband not to hold his wife “to harm her” (2:231). Two witnesses are called for (65:2). A woman may also seek release (khulʿ), as in a report in Sahih al-Bukhari where Thabit ibn Qays’s wife was granted it on returning his garden.
misread: That a Muslim man may divorce at will and the woman has no recourse.
sources: The Prophet is reported to have said that of lawful things, divorce is the most hated to God (Abu Dawud, a report some scholars grade weak). Schools differ on the “triple divorce” in one sitting and on the wife’s right to a judicial dissolution. Many modern family laws require a court or waiting period.

title: Diya
def: Blood money: compensation paid to the family of a person killed unintentionally, and sometimes accepted in place of retaliation.
what: “It is not for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake, and whoever kills a believer by mistake must free a believing slave and pay blood money to his family” (4:92). The same verse applies it when the dead person belonged to a people with whom there is a treaty. For intentional killing the Quran sets equal retaliation, but praises pardon (2:178, 5:45).

title: Dogs
def: The Quran allows hunting with trained dogs; hadith differ on the dog’s ritual purity, and the Prophet taught kindness to them.
what: “They ask you what is lawful. Say: the good things, and what you have taught the trained hunting animals” (5:4). The dog of the cave’s sleepers is mentioned in 18:18. The Prophet said a man was forgiven for giving water to a thirsty dog (Sahih al-Bukhari). The schools differ on whether a dog’s saliva makes things unclean, the Malikis holding that it does not.
sources: A hadith says that angels do not enter a house with a dog (Sahih al-Bukhari), and that dogs which are not working animals are discouraged in the home. Many Muslim societies are unfriendly to dogs, and many Muslims keep them as guard dogs, shepherds, or pets.

title: Dome of the Rock
def: The shrine on the Temple Mount in Jerusalem, completed in 691–692 by the caliph Abd al-Malik, with some of the oldest inscriptions of the Quran.
what: Its inscriptions include Quranic verses on God’s oneness (112), on Jesus as the Messiah and servant of God (4:171) and “the religion with God is Islam” (3:19), and the declaration that Muhammad is the messenger of God. The Dome stands over the rock from which Muslim tradition says the Prophet ascended, while the mosque al-Aqsa is a separate building at the southern end of the platform.
misread: That its inscriptions are hostile to Jews and Christians.
sources: The wording on Jesus is an affirmation: “the Messiah Jesus, son of Mary, was only a messenger of God, and His word which He cast into Mary, and a spirit from Him” (4:171), with the warning not to say “three”. Historians see in it a statement of Islam addressed to the Christians of Jerusalem, whose great domed church was nearby.

title: Domestic discipline (Quran 4:34)
def: The verse on men’s responsibility in the family which includes the word “strike”; its meaning has been debated and restricted by many scholars.
what: The verse says men are responsible for women (qawwāmūn), and for wives who show ill will it gives steps: advise them, leave them in bed, and “iḍribūhunna” (4:34). The next verse (4:35) calls for arbiters from both families. “Strike” is the usual translation, and some read the word as “separate from them”.
misread: That Islam allows a husband to beat his wife.
sources: Classical commentators set limits. Ibn Abbas said it should be with a tooth-stick, a symbolic touch; the Prophet in his Farewell Sermon said “not severely” (Sahih Muslim); and no striking of the face. Aisha said he never struck a woman or a servant (Sahih Muslim), and he condemned any man who beats his wife as he would a slave and then lies with her (Sahih al-Bukhari). He said: “the best of you are the best to their wives” (al-Tirmidhi). Many contemporary scholars say that violence is a crime, and that the verse’s steps have to be understood in this light.

title: Domination of Islam
def: Verses such as 9:33 say God sent the Prophet “to make it prevail over all religion”; commentators differ on what “prevail” means.
what: “It is He who sent His messenger with guidance and the religion of truth, to make it prevail over all religion, even if the polytheists dislike it” (9:33, 48:28, 61:9). Some commentators take it to mean prevailing by proof and argument, others by the end-time return of Jesus, and others in the sense of political success.
sources: Muslim scholars read this with the verse “no compulsion in religion” (2:256), so that prevailing does not mean forcing belief. The word can also mean that the truth becomes clear.

title: Dowry
def: The gift a husband gives his wife on marriage, which is hers alone.
what: “Give women their dowries as a gift” (4:4). The husband may not take it back, “even if you have given one of them a heap of gold” (4:20). It is the wife’s property, and not her father’s or her husband’s. The amount is whatever is agreed. The Prophet told a man who had nothing to give to teach his bride what he knew of the Quran (Sahih al-Bukhari).

title: Dreams
def: In Islam a true dream can be a good tiding, and the Quran tells the dreams of Joseph and the king of Egypt.
what: Joseph tells his father of eleven stars, the sun and the moon bowing to him (12:4). He interprets the king’s dream of seven fat cows and seven lean ones (12:43–49). The Prophet said that a good dream is one forty-sixth part of prophecy (Sahih al-Bukhari). He distinguished the good dream, which comes from God, from the bad dream, which comes from Satan.

title: Du Wenxiu
def: A Hui Muslim leader (1823–1872) who led the Panthay rebellion against the Qing in Yunnan, and ruled from Dali as “Sultan Sulayman”.
what: Du Wenxiu led a rising of Hui Muslims in Yunnan from 1856, after years of massacres and persecution, set up a state at Dali, and took the title Sulayman. The Qing army took Dali in 1872, and he was executed.

title: Du'a
def: Prayer of supplication: asking God directly for what one needs.
what: “When My servants ask you about Me, I am near; I answer the call of the caller when he calls” (2:186). “Call upon Me; I will respond” (40:60). The Prophet said that supplication is worship (al-Tirmidhi). It can be made at any time, in any language, and needs no intermediary.
sources: The Muslim understanding is close to the verse in Matthew (“ask and it will be given to you”). The difference on which Islam insists is that one asks God directly, without a saint or priest between.

title: Dalal
def: The verbal noun of ḍalla: error, going astray from God’s guidance.
what: Ḍalāl is the noun for the act of ḍalla, to go astray. Faruqi lists it simply as the verbal noun of that verb. It names the state of someone who has strayed from the straight path that God has shown. The Quran uses it in several settings. It warns those who turn away from God’s message, and in the Fatiha the believers ask to be guided to the straight path, not that of those who have gone astray (1:7). The word is therefore tied to the main petition of every prayer. In ordinary Arabic it can mean being lost in a literal sense, and the Quran uses it of both senses.
misread: That it means only “sin” in the sense of a moral lapse, when it describes losing the way altogether.

title: Dall
def: A person who errs and strays from God’s straight path, especially in the course of history; plural ḍāllūn.
what: Ḍāll is the active participle of ḍalla: one who has gone astray. Faruqi describes him as a person who strays from the straight path of God, especially as that falls within human history. The plural is ḍāllūn, which takes the form ḍāllīn when it follows a preposition or serves as an object. The word is a general description of error and carries no claim about any one group.

The word occurs in the last verse of the Fatiha, where Muslims ask to be guided to the straight path and not the path of those who have earned anger or of those who have gone astray (al-ḍāllīn) (1:7). Since the chapter is recited in every cycle of prayer, every Muslim repeats this petition many times a day. Interpreters differ on whom the phrase singles out, and many read it as a warning against all error.
misread: That the word is an insult for non-Muslims, when it names a condition of straying that anyone can fall into.
sources: Some early commentators related the two groups in 1:7 to particular communities, while others read both as general types of error.

title: Dalla
def: To err and stray from the straight path of God revealed to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him).
what: Ḍalla means to lose the way, and so to err and stray. Faruqi uses it for straying from the straight path of God that was revealed to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). The related noun is ḍalāl and the participle is ḍāll. The Quran uses the verb in both literal and moral senses. It says that whoever follows guidance does so for his own good, and whoever goes astray does so to his own loss (17:15). The verse adds that no soul bears the burden of another. The word thus sets individual responsibility next to guidance: each person chooses whether to follow or to stray.
misread: That it names a permanent state, when the Quran treats going astray as something a person can turn from.

title: Din, al-
def: The normative, perfect religion that God ordained for humanity, covering faith, ethics, law, worship, institutions and judgment.
what: Al-dīn is the word for religion, but it is wider than the English term. Faruqi defines it as the norm, the perfect way God ordained for humankind. It includes belief, ethics, law, devotion, institutions and the final reckoning. Religion in the narrow sense of private belief does not capture it. The Quran says that the dīn with God is Islam (3:19). At the end of the Prophet’s mission it says that God has perfected the dīn for believers and completed His favour on them (5:3). The word also means judgment, as in yawm al-dīn, the Day of Judgment (1:4), where the same root points to accountability.
misread: That it translates as “religion” in the sense of a private matter, when it is a whole way of life with a day of reckoning.
sources: The root d-y-n carries the senses of obedience, debt and judgment, which scholars find joined in the single concept.

title: Dirayah al-Hadith
def: The studies concerned with the validity of the reporting of the Prophet’s words and acts, and of what is reported.
what: Dirāyah al-ḥadīth is the branch of study that tests the reliability of reports from the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). Faruqi lists it among the sciences and describes it as the study of the validity of the reporting and of what is reported. Its counterpart is riwāyah al-ḥadīth, the work of transmitting the reports themselves. Its methods include examining the chain of narrators (isnād), judging the character and memory of each narrator, and comparing a report with the Quran and with other reports. The science gave Muslims a framework for sorting sound reports from weak and fabricated ones. The great collections, such as those of al-Bukhari and Muslim, were compiled using such criteria.
misread: That hadith were accepted without any checking, when scholars built a detailed science of verification.

title: Duha, al-
def: The part of the day from when the sun has risen high until noon, and the name of the supererogatory prayer offered in that time.
what: Al-ḍuḥā is the forenoon, once the sun has climbed well above the horizon and the morning is bright. The Quran swears by it at the opening of surah 93, which is named al-Ḍuḥā: “By the morning brightness” (93:1). The time ends as the sun reaches its height at midday, when the noon prayer approaches. Many Muslims treat this bright part of the day as a good time for work and for remembrance.

Muslims also use the word for the voluntary prayer offered in this period, called ṣalāt al-ḍuḥā. It is not obligatory. Abu Dharr reported that the Prophet said two rakʿas of ḍuḥā are enough to stand for the charity owed by every joint of the body each day (Sahih Muslim). Most people pray two to eight rakʿas, a number that scholars treat as a matter of choice.
misread: Often rendered simply as “morning”, which blurs the exact span the term names: after sunrise has become full daylight and before noon.

title: Dunya, al-
def: The nearer life of this world, whose values rank below those of the Hereafter, and by extension a life given over to pursuing such values.
what: Al-dunyā comes from a root meaning “nearer” or “lower”. It is the life in front of us, set against al-ākhira, the life to come. The Quran calls it “only the enjoyment of delusion” when it becomes the whole aim of a person (3:185), and says: “This worldly life is nothing but diversion and play; the home of the Hereafter is the true life” (29:64).

The term therefore carries a judgment of value as well as of place. A person described as devoted to al-dunyā has made the lower goods of wealth, rank and comfort the center of life. The Quran does not forbid the good things of this world, and asks believers for “good in this world and good in the Hereafter” (2:201). The fault lies in letting the lower values rule.
misread: Rendered “the world” or “worldliness”, which loses the contrast of nearer and lower values against those of the Hereafter that the Arabic holds.
